_help: speaker: narrator (bottom panel) | scientist (Nova pops in; optional expression + body, see nova.json) | equipment (speech bubble). Add, delete or reorder lines freely. quiz.answer is the letter of the right option (A = first). image: the drawn art in the gold frame (no extension needed; {x} = the x1/x2/x3 folder). moreInfo.image: the real photo(s) in the "i" card, default assets/image/real_equipment/{x}/ (add -1, -2, … for a gallery); leave it empty to use the default. moreInfo.imageCredit: small credit under the photo. moreInfo.text: the summary paragraph. moreInfo.funFacts (optional): a list of short facts, one bullet each, e.g. ["Fact one.", "Fact two."]. moreInfo.sources (optional): a list of web addresses (shown as the site name, e.g. NASA Science) or { "label": "NASA Science: Viking 1", "url": "https://…" }; links open in a new tab. Optional "voice": this equipment's voice file, e.g. assets/mp3/vocal/equipment/equipment_low_pitch (none = sounds.voices.equipment in assets.json). See README §4. Text formatting in any "text" or "greeting": italic, bold, smaller, the other connected equipment speaking (own line, italic, smaller, faded, quieter voice), e.g. "Hah, tell us about it. Hmph… Can't believe them… We're still here! Still standing!". Optional "chorusVoice" on a line: another voice file for its part. See README §2. Copy full examples from equipment/_examples/.
name: InSight Lander

script.speaker: equipment
script.text: ...You may call me InSight. As you were saying?.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: In 2018, NASA launched InSight on an Atlas V rocket from California, the first mission ever sent to study what’s deep inside Mars.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: It was a three-legged lander with a long robot arm, a super-sensitive quake detector and a heat probe, powered by two round solar panels that soaked up sunlight.

script.speaker: scientist
script.text: What are you doing? And why do I have to be quiet...?

script.speaker: equipment
script.text: I listen to the heartbeat of this planet. Every little quake of its surface. I study what makes Mars… Mars. The wind clears the dust off my panels, and I wait patiently.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Its mission was to measure Mars’s marsquakes, heat and wobble while staying perfectly still, until dust slowly covered its solar panels and it ran out of power in December 2022.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: It recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes and the sound of Martian wind, which let scientists measure the size of Mars’s crust, mantle and liquid metal core for the first time.

script.speaker: scientist
script.text: That’s… so cool… I won’t disturb you anymore...

script.speaker: equipment
script.text: Huhu, please, you can speak a little louder than that. It's no problem at all.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: InSight launched from Vandenberg, California, on 5 May 2018 at 4:05 a.m. local time, flew about 485 million km, landed on 26 November 2018 on a flat plain called Elysium Planitia, and has now been on Mars for 8 years.

moreInfo.text: InSight was a NASA lander built to study the inside of Mars: its crust, mantle and core. It launched in May 2018 and landed in November 2018 on Elysium Planitia, a flat, safe plain near the equator. Its robot arm placed a super-sensitive seismometer and a heat probe on the ground, like a doctor checking the planet’s pulse, temperature and reflexes. Over four years it recorded more than a thousand marsquakes, until dust on its solar panels ended the mission in December 2022.
funFacts: InSight was the first NASA mission to another planet ever launched from the West Coast of the USA.
Its seismometer felt more than 1,300 marsquakes, showing that Mars is still shaking today.
InSight recorded the sound of the wind on Mars, a low rumble from winds blowing at about 10 to 15 mph.
Its robot arm was 1.8 metres long, longer than most grown-ups are tall!
Two briefcase-sized mini spacecraft called MarCO flew to Mars alongside it, the first tiny CubeSats ever sent to another planet.
Its heat probe, nicknamed “the mole”, was meant to dig deep underground, but the Martian soil clumped together and it couldn’t get a grip.
Its marsquake data showed that the inside of Mars is lumpy, full of chunks of rock from ancient impacts.

questions.question: How did InSight get to Mars?
options: On a Titan rocket launched from Florida
On an Atlas V rocket launched from California
On two Delta II rockets
Inside a Saturn V with astronauts
questions.explanation: InSight launched on an Atlas V rocket from Vandenberg in California. (A Titan rocket from Florida carried Viking 1.)

questions.question: What was InSight made of, and what powered it?
options: A small battery-powered car
A six-wheeled rover powered by a nuclear generator
A three-legged lander with a robot arm and a quake detector, powered by solar panels
An orbiter powered by the wind
questions.explanation: InSight was a lander with three legs, a long robot arm and science instruments, powered by two round solar panels.

questions.question: What did InSight’s marsquake data let scientists measure for the first time?
options: The height of Mars’s tallest mountain
How many moons Mars has
The size of Mars’s crust, mantle and core
The colour of Mars’s sky
questions.explanation: Marsquake waves travel through the planet, so they revealed the size of its crust, mantle and liquid metal core.

questions.question: When did InSight blast off?
options: 5 May 2008, at 4:05 in the morning
26 November 2018, at 11:52 in the morning
20 August 1975, at 5:22 in the evening
5 May 2018, at 4:05 in the morning
questions.explanation: InSight launched on 5 May 2018 at 4:05 a.m. California time. 26 November 2018 was the day it landed.

questions.question: Why is InSight still on Mars, and how long has it been there?
options: It was built to stay still and listen, until dust covered its solar panels, and it’s been 8 years
It got stuck in sand while driving, and it’s been 22 years
A wrong command from Earth cut it off, and it’s been 50 years
Astronauts switched it off, and it’s been 3 years
questions.explanation: InSight never moved. Dust slowly covered its solar panels until it ran out of power in 2022. It landed in 2018, 8 years ago.
